result:
The morning arrived without permission and settled over the town. I woke before the alarm and listened to distant rain. Somewhere a kettle clicked off and left a small silence. My shoes waited beside the door like patient old dogs. I thought about leaving and then thought about staying longer. The street outside was empty except for one determined cyclist. She wore yellow gloves and pedaled straight through the puddles. I admired her certainty and envied her simple clear direction. My own map had folded itself into an unreadable square. Still I packed a bag and chose the left road.

The left road climbed gently past hedges and sleeping houses. A cat watched me from a wall without blinking once. I nodded politely because manners matter even toward silent cats. Beyond the houses the fields opened wide under grey light. Wind moved through grass like fingers searching for lost keys. I remembered childhood summers spent hiding in exactly such fields. We built forts from branches and declared them sovereign nations. Our laws concerned biscuits, secrets, and never surrendering before dinner. Time was generous then and we spent it without counting. Now I count everything including steps, regrets, and remaining sandwiches.

At noon I reached a village with one crooked shop. The shopkeeper sold maps, marmalade, umbrellas, and dubious local advice. He pointed north and warned me about the singing bridge. Bridges should not sing, I said, but he only shrugged. Some bridges remember footsteps, he answered, and hum them back. I bought marmalade anyway and thanked him for the mystery. Outside, children chased a hoop down the sloping high street. Their laughter bounced off stone walls and startled the pigeons. For a moment the whole village seemed briefly, perfectly awake. Then clouds returned and everyone remembered their ordinary afternoon errands.

The bridge appeared after a mile of birches and mud. It crossed a river that moved darkly beneath bare branches. I stepped onto the planks and heard a low note. Another step produced another note, slightly higher and oddly mournful. I walked slowly, composing a tune with my muddy boots. Perhaps the bridge remembered soldiers, lovers, merchants, and wandering fools. Perhaps it simply sang because rivers teach wood to resonate. Either explanation satisfied me while I stood listening midstream alone. The water below carried leaves toward some distant unseen sea. I wished them well and continued toward the northern hills.

Hills always look gentle until you are actually climbing them. My legs protested in two languages and invented several more. Halfway up I stopped beside a stone shaped like bread. I ate marmalade sandwiches there and felt absurdly, defiantly happy. Happiness rarely announces itself; it sits beside you eating crumbs. From the summit, valleys unfolded in overlapping shades of green. A train stitched silver thread across the farthest valley floor. People inside were reading, sleeping, dreaming toward their own destinations. I waved although nobody could possibly see my small gesture. Some gestures matter precisely because nobody witnesses them except ourselves.

Descending took longer because knees remember every careless year vividly. In the next town, rain finally caught up with me. I sheltered under an awning beside a florist closing early. She gave me a bruised rose and refused any payment. It will perish tonight anyway, she said with cheerful fatalism. I carried the rose carefully through streets smelling of rain. An old man shared his umbrella without asking my name. We discussed weather, football, and the unreliable nature of knees. At the station he vanished into steam and evening crowds. I never learned where he was going or coming from.

The train north was warm, crowded, and smelled of coats. Across from me sat a woman knitting something impossibly large. It might become a sweater, blanket, sail, or small house. She laughed when asked and said possibilities keep yarn interesting. Beside her, a boy drew dragons on the fogged window. Each dragon breathed little clouds that merged with real fog. When the train slowed, he erased them with his sleeve. Creation and destruction shared one sleeve without any apparent grief. I offered him marmalade, but he preferred drawing edible dragons. His mother smiled apologetically and accepted a sandwich for herself.

Night gathered outside while lamps made islands inside the carriage. Reflections doubled every passenger into a slightly more mysterious twin. I saw myself holding a wilting rose and looking thoughtful. Thoughtful is sometimes just tired wearing its best available coat. The conductor announced a station whose name I misheard completely. It sounded like somewhere invented for people needing second chances. On impulse, I gathered my bag and stepped into darkness. The platform was empty except for moths orbiting one lamp. A sign creaked, revealing the town name: Little Nowhere, perhaps. Perfect, I thought, because nowhere often hides the best somewheres.

The only inn had a fire, soup, and no vacancies. The innkeeper considered my rose and offered her greenhouse instead. Sleep among tomatoes, she suggested, and ignore the snoring cucumbers. I accepted gratefully and slept beneath glass freckled with stars. Plants breathe differently at night, slower and somehow more honest. I dreamed the singing bridge led directly to my childhood. My younger self waited midstream, demanding biscuits and clear explanations. I had none to offer except marmalade and this rose. He accepted both, then pushed me gently toward waking life. Morning found tomatoes ripening and my shoes damp with dew.

I left money, thanks, and one button on the counter. Buttons fall like small moons from coats traveling too far. Outside, the town revealed orchards, a library, and one bakery. I traded my last sandwich for a warm cinnamon roll. The baker asked where I was ultimately heading this week. I admitted I had mistaken wandering for a destination again. She nodded wisely and pointed toward the sea beyond town. Everyone ends there eventually, either for answers or for swimming. So I walked onward, rose gone, heart inexplicably lighter now. The road ahead sang quietly underneath my tired, willing feet.
